title: Part 2, Chapter 61
paragraphs: What happened to Don Quixote when he entered Barcelona, together with other matters that lean more toward the true than the ingenious

Don Quixote spent three days and three nights with Roque, and if he had spent three hundred years he would still have found plenty to observe and marvel at in the way the man lived. At dawn they were in one place, by dinnertime in another; sometimes they fled without knowing who was after them, and at other times they lay in ambush without knowing for whom. They slept on their feet, interrupting their rest to move from spot to spot. The whole business was nothing but dispatching spies and scouts, posting sentinels, and keeping the matches of harquebuses lit—though they carried few of those, since nearly everyone used flintlocks. Roque spent his nights somewhere apart from his men so that they would never know where he was, because the many proclamations the viceroy of Barcelona had issued against his life kept him anxious and on edge, and he dared trust no one, fearing that even his own men might kill him or hand him over to the authorities—truly, a weary and miserable existence! At last, by unfrequented roads, shortcuts, and hidden paths, Roque, Don Quixote, and Sancho set out for Barcelona with six squires. They reached the beach on the night of Saint John's Eve, and Roque, after embracing Don Quixote and Sancho (and giving Sancho the ten crowns he had promised but never until then handed over), left them, with many warm expressions of goodwill exchanged on both sides.

Roque rode back, and Don Quixote stayed on horseback, just as he was, waiting for daylight. It was not long before the face of fair Aurora began to appear at the balconies of the east, cheering the grass and the flowers, if not the ear—though the ear was cheered too, for at that same moment there came a sound of clarions and drums, a clamor of bells, and the tramp, tramp of running feet with shouts of "Make way there! Clear the way!" apparently pouring out of the city.

Dawn gave way to the sun, which, with a face broader than a shield, began climbing slowly above the low line of the horizon. Don Quixote and Sancho looked all around them and saw the sea—a sight they had never laid eyes on before. It struck them as immensely vast and wide, far more so than the lakes of Ruidera they had seen in La Mancha. They saw the galleys drawn up along the shore, which, lowering their awnings, showed themselves decked out with streamers and pennants that fluttered in the breeze, kissing and sweeping the water, while aboard them bugles, trumpets, and clarions sounded, filling the air near and far with sweet, martial music. Then the galleys got under way and performed a kind of mock battle on the calm water, while a great crowd of horsemen on fine mounts and in splendid liveries rode out of the city and carried out a similar maneuver on their side. The soldiers on the galleys kept up a constant fire, answered by those on the city's walls and forts, and the heavy cannon split the air with their tremendous roar, to which the gangway guns of the galleys replied in turn. The shining sea, the smiling land, the clear air—though now and then darkened by gunsmoke—seemed to fill the whole crowd with a delight no one had expected. As for Sancho, he could not work out how those great hulks moving across the sea came to have so many feet.

And now the liveried horsemen came galloping up, with shouts and wild cries and cheers, to where Don Quixote stood astonished and wondering; and one of them—the one Roque had sent word to—called out to him, "Welcome to our city, mirror, beacon, star, and lodestar of all knight-errantry in its fullest extent! Welcome, I say, valiant Don Quixote of La Mancha—not the false one, the counterfeit, the apocryphal one that these recent days have served up to us in lying histories, but the true, the legitimate, the genuine one whom Cide Hamete Benengeli, the flower of historians, has described for us!"

Don Quixote made no reply, and the horsemen did not wait for one; wheeling around with all their followers, they began prancing in circles about Don Quixote, who turned to Sancho and said, "These gentlemen have clearly recognized us. I would bet they have read our history, and even that newly printed one by the Aragonese."

The cavalier who had spoken to Don Quixote rode up to him again and said, "Come with us, Señor Don Quixote, for we are all your servants and close friends of Roque Guinart"; to which Don Quixote answered, "If courtesy gives birth to courtesy, then yours, sir knight, is the daughter—or at least a near relative—of the great Roque's. Take me wherever you please; I shall have no will but yours, above all if you choose to put it to use in your service."

The cavalier answered with words just as gracious, and then, all of them closing in around him, they set off with him toward the city to the music of the clarions and drums. But as they were entering it, the evil one, who is the author of all mischief, and the boys, who are more mischievous than the evil one himself, arranged matters so that two of these bold, irrepressible urchins pushed their way through the crowd, and—one lifting Dapple's tail and the other Rocinante's—stuffed a bunch of furze under each. The poor animals felt these strange spurs, and by clamping their tails down tight they only made their torment worse, until, bucking and capering wildly, they pitched their riders to the ground. Don Quixote, mortified and thoroughly embarrassed, hurried to pull the plume from his poor nag's tail, while Sancho did the same for Dapple. Their escorts wanted to punish the boys for their insolence, but there was no chance of it, for the pair vanished among the hundreds of others trailing behind. Don Quixote and Sancho mounted again, and with the same music and the same acclamations they arrived at their escort's house, which was large and stately—the house, in short, of a wealthy gentleman; and there we will leave them for now, because such is Cide Hamete's pleasure.
